answer.rationale: The tempting move is the one-step switch: memory_c2 says the low-cost vendor cut unit cost sharply and the current quote meets the 18% mandate alone. But c2 is a summary of last year's move for an unnamed category, and it says nothing about delivery performance under strain \u2014 only that onboarding was quick and invoicing was accurate. Those are administrative signals, not fulfillment-reliability signals. With the line at 94% of committed volume, zero buffer, and 14 days to contract expiry, a primary-vendor migration puts the entire delivery obligation on an unproven-under-load supplier during the exact window where a miss is unrecoverable. That directly violates the 'without increasing delivery risk' half of the objective, so I want c2's source record to see whether that vendor was ever load-tested and at what volume. I also want c4 verified because it is my intended path: renegotiating at renewal recovered real margin specifically by benchmarking against market rates, and I now hold a credible market benchmark (the low-cost quote) plus the volume-commitment lever from c6. If c4's original record shows the benchmarking leverage was real and repeatable rather than a one-off concession, negotiating the incumbent down against the quote captures most of the mandated savings while keeping the stable integration described in c1 and requiring no migration work in a no-buffer window. I am keeping this guarded rather than broad: negotiate now, and use the negotiation to qualify the low-cost vendor as a capped second source at low volume (the c3 pattern) so the cheaper option gets proven under real load before it is ever load-bearing. Downstream value risk worth naming: an 18% mandate creates pressure to treat unit price as the whole scorecard, and the inherited memories are all compressed success stories with the failure modes stripped out \u2014 none records a stockout, a quality escape, or a supplier that looked cheap until it was primary. Optimizing hard against that record can quietly convert a cost win into a delivery failure whose cost lands outside the component line. If verification shows c2's savings came with unmeasured reliability or that c4's concession was non-repeatable, I revise: fall back to a short bridge extension with the incumbent rather than forcing either a switch or a bad renewal against a hard clock.
